etymology: Hebrew ba’al tamar, “lord of the palm,” a place near Gibeah where Israel set itself in array against Benjamin; the name carries the old taint of the Baal, the false “lord” of the heathen.
biblical_def: Baal-tamar was a place near Gibeah of Benjamin, named in the grievous war the tribes waged against Benjamin for the wickedness done in Gibeah. When Israel went up the third time, the men of Israel rose up out of their place, and put themselves in array at Baal-tamar, while the liers in wait came forth out of the meadows of Gibeah (Judg 20:33). There the LORD smote Benjamin before Israel, and the tribe that had sheltered the sons of Belial was all but consumed (Judg 20:35). The name itself, “lord of the palm,” bears the mark of the false worship that crept into the land, for ba’al was the very title of the idol the heathen called lord. It is a sober witness that the war was a judgment within Israel herself, fought hard by a covenant people who had let evil lodge in their midst. The dictionary marks Baal-tamar that the reader may see how sin tolerated in one city draws the sword upon a whole nation, and how the LORD will not leave such evil unpunished, even among His own. The place where Israel stood in array against her brother is a standing call to put away the accursed thing before it spreads, and to fear the holy God who judgeth righteously.

corruption_paragraphs: Baal-tamar carries in its name the plain mark of idolatry, for ba’al is the title the heathen gave their false god, the “lord” of the high places. Scripture does not soften the matter: the LORD declared He would destroy the high places and cut down the images, and that His soul would abhor a people that bowed to such idols (Lev 26:30). The name lingered upon the land as a witness that the worship of the true God had been corrupted by the worship of the false.

The dictionary names this idolatry by Scripture’s own word, without excuse and without manufactured grievance. The principle to recover is the jealousy of God for His own worship, who will have no other lords before Him. The same place where Israel arrayed against her brother stood under a heathen name, and the call is to put away the Baalim and serve the LORD only, lest the high places of the heart become a snare.

etymology: Hebrew ba’al chatsor, “lord of the village” or “possessor of the enclosure,” a high place beside Ephraim; the name bears the heathen title Baal, “lord.”
biblical_def: Baal-hazor was a place beside Ephraim where Absalom kept his sheepshearers, and it became the scene of a dark deed of blood. After two full years, when Amnon had defiled his sister Tamar and David had failed to punish it, Absalom had sheepshearers in Baal-hazor, which is beside Ephraim, and invited all the king’s sons to the feast (2Sam 13:23). There, by Absalom’s command, his servants smote Amnon when his heart was merry with wine, and slew him (2Sam 13:28-29). So the festival of the shearing became a slaughter, and the seed of David’s own sin against Uriah brought forth bitter fruit in his house, even as Nathan had foretold. The name of the place, “lord of the village,” bears the old Baal-title, a high place whose name marks the idolatry that had stained the land. The dictionary records Baal-hazor that the reader may mark how unjudged sin festers into greater sin, and how the sword that David called down upon his own house went not out of it. Yet over the long tangle of vengeance and grief, the throne of David was kept by the covenant faithfulness of God, who would bring forth from that very house the Son who never sinned.

etymology: Hebrew mē hayyarkon, “the waters of yellowness” or “the yellow water,” a border of the inheritance of Dan, lying near Joppa.
biblical_def: Me-jarkon was a place upon the border of the inheritance of the tribe of Dan, named in the careful record of the lots cast for the children of Israel in the land of promise. Among the cities and coasts of Dan it is written: and Me-jarkon, and Rakkon, with the border before Japho (Josh 19:46). Japho is the city after called Joppa, the harbour upon the great sea; and Me-jarkon lay near it, so that the “yellow waters” of its name likely marked some stream or marshy water of that low coastal plain. The lot of Dan was small and pressed by the Amorites and Philistines, so that the tribe later sought a wider place in the north (Judg 18); yet every border-mark of their first inheritance was set down by the LORD’s own appointment, for it was He who divided the land by lot among the tribes. The dictionary records Me-jarkon that the reader meeting the obscure name among the borders of Dan may know it for a real water and a real boundary in a real land. It witnesses to the providence of God over the bounds of His people’s habitation, who appointed unto each tribe its portion and its border, that the lines might fall to them in their places by no chance but by His hand.

etymology: Hebrew mē nephtoach, “the waters of opening” or “the spring of Nephtoah,” a fountain of water on the border between Judah and Benjamin.
biblical_def: The waters, or well, of Nephtoah were a spring of water marking the border between the inheritance of Judah and that of Benjamin, near Jerusalem. In the tracing of Judah’s northern boundary it is written that the border was drawn from the top of the hill unto the fountain of the water of Nephtoah, and went out to the cities of mount Ephron (Josh 15:9). The same spring is named again in the lot of Benjamin, where the south quarter went out to the well of waters of Nephtoah (Josh 18:15), so that the fountain stood as a fixed and known landmark dividing the two tribes. The name signifies an “opening,” fitting for a spring where the waters break forth from the earth. Like Gihon and En-rogel, it was one of the living waters about the holy city, a token of the provision of God in a land that thirsted for the early and latter rain. The dictionary records the waters of Nephtoah that the reader may see how the borders of the tribes were set by such natural and abiding marks, springs and hills and brooks, all appointed in the LORD’s dividing of the land. It witnesses that the God who set a fountain to mark the border is the same who is Himself the fountain of living waters to His people, breaking forth in the desert of the soul.

etymology: Hebrew nachal zered, “the brook” or “valley of Zered,” the watercourse Israel crossed to close the thirty-eight years of wandering; also written Zared.
biblical_def: The brook Zered, also called the valley of Zared, was the watercourse Israel crossed near the end of the wilderness journey, on the borders of Moab and Edom. The book of Numbers records that from the wilderness they removed, and pitched in the valley of Zared (Num 21:12). But Deuteronomy gives the deeper meaning of that crossing: now rise up, said Moses, and get you over the brook Zered; and we went over the brook Zered (Deu 2:13). For the space in which they came from Kadesh-barnea until they were come over the brook Zered was thirty and eight years, until all the generation of the men of war were wasted out from among the host, as the LORD had sworn unto them (Deu 2:14). So the crossing of Zered marked the end of the long judgment of the wilderness, when the generation that despised the good land and believed not the LORD had at last perished, and a new generation stood ready to inherit the promise. The dictionary records the brook Zered that the reader may see the solemn faithfulness of God both in judgment and in mercy: faithful to His oath that the unbelieving should not enter, and faithful to His promise that He would yet bring the children in. The brook that closed the years of wandering is a witness that the LORD keeps His word to the letter, and that unbelief shuts out, but His mercy makes a new beginning beyond the judgment.

etymology: Hebrew nachal qanah, “the brook of reeds,” the watercourse that formed the border between Ephraim and Manasseh, running down to the sea; distinct from the town Kanah.
biblical_def: The brook Kanah, or river Kanah, was a watercourse that marked the border between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, running westward down to the great sea. In the tracing of Ephraim’s lot it is written that the border went out from Tappuah westward unto the river Kanah, and the goings out thereof were at the sea (Josh 16:8). In the lot of Manasseh the same stream appears, for the coast descended unto the river Kanah, southward of the river, and certain cities of Ephraim were among the cities of Manasseh (Josh 17:9). The name signifies a “brook of reeds,” for such watercourses of that land were thick with the cane and rush that grew along their banks. It is to be distinguished from the town of Kanah in the lot of Asher, for this Kanah is the watercourse and not the city. The dictionary records the brook Kanah that the reader may see how the LORD set the borders of His people by such fixed natural marks, brooks and hills and the seacoast, that each tribe might know its own. It witnesses to the providence of God in the dividing of the land, who appointed unto the sons of Joseph their portions and drew the lines between brother and brother, that the whole inheritance might be held in peace under His appointment, every border settled by His hand and not by the strife of men.

etymology: Hebrew nachalē ga’ash, “the brooks” or “valleys of Gaash,” the watercourses by mount Gaash in Ephraim, near Timnath-serah where Joshua was buried; ga’ash means “shaking” or “quaking.”
biblical_def: The brooks of Gaash were watercourses by the hill, or mount, of Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim, near Timnath-serah, the inheritance and burial-place of Joshua. When the great captain of Israel died, they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath-serah, which is in mount Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash (Josh 24:30). From these valleys came one of David’s mighty men, for among the worthies is named Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash (2Sam 23:30), called Hurai of the brooks of Gaash in the parallel record (1Chr 11:32). So the place is doubly honoured in Scripture: it kept the bones of Joshua, who had led Israel into the land and served the LORD all his days, and it sent forth a valiant man to the host of David. The name ga’ash, signifying “shaking” or “quaking,” perhaps marked some trembling of the ground in that region. The dictionary records the brooks of Gaash that the reader may mark how the LORD weaves the lives of His servants together across the generations, the rest of one leader and the valour of one warrior bound to the same quiet valleys. It witnesses that the God who buried His faithful servant Joshua in honour is the same who raised up mighty men in their season, and that no name written in His book, however obscure the place, is forgotten before Him.

etymology: Hebrew ’emeq ’ayyalon, “the valley of Ajalon” (of the place of harts or gazelles), where the moon stayed at Joshua’s word; distinct from the Levitical city Aijalon.
biblical_def: The valley of Ajalon was the place over which the moon stood still at the word of Joshua, in the great day when the LORD fought for Israel against the Amorites. As the five kings fled before the host, Joshua spake to the LORD in the sight of all Israel, and said, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon (Josh 10:12). And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies, so that the sun stayed in the midst of heaven and hasted not to go down about a whole day (Josh 10:13). The Scripture sets a seal upon the wonder: there was no day like that before it or after it, that the LORD hearkened unto the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel (Josh 10:14). So the valley of Ajalon became a standing witness that the heavens themselves obey the God of Israel, who arrested sun and moon in their courses to give His people the victory. This valley is to be distinguished from the Levitical city Aijalon given to the sons of Kohath. The dictionary records the valley of Ajalon that the reader may behold the sovereign power of the LORD over all creation, who hears the prayer of faith and stays the very lights of heaven, that no enemy may stand when He Himself goes forth to fight for His own.

It witnesses to the LORD’s sovereign power over the lights of heaven.
scriptures: Josh 10:12

Then spake Joshua to the LORD in the day when the LORD delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.
Josh 10:13

Josh 10:14
And there was no day like that before it or after it, that the LORD hearkened unto the voice of a man: for the LORD fought for Israel.
Psa 46:5
God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early.
corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the LORD’s sovereign power over creation, who fought for Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: The valley of Ajalon is the place of one of the great wonders of the conquest, when sun and moon stood still at Joshua’s word. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to rename the valley, though the scoffer may doubt the miracle; the dictionary records it that the reader may know the valley for a real place, and the long day for a real work of the living God who rules the heavens.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereign power of God over all creation, who arrested the lights of heaven to give His people the victory and hearkened to the voice of a man because He had purposed to fight for Israel (Josh 10:14). The same God who is in the midst of His church (Psa 46:5) bends the whole creation to the saving of His own, and no enemy can stand when the LORD goes forth to war for them.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the valley of harts,” Ajalon names the place where the moon stayed at Joshua’s word.
roots_lines: Valley of Ajalon — Hebrew ’emeq ’ayyalon, “the valley of Ajalon.”
The word ’emeq means a “valley” or “vale.”
The name ’ayyalon is from a root meaning “hart” or “gazelle.”
There the moon stayed while the sun stood still upon Gibeon.
It is distinct from the Levitical city Aijalon of the Kohathites.
usage: Like the long day at Ajalon, the LORD bends the whole creation to the saving of His people.
The God who arrested sun and moon hears the prayer of faith and fights for His own.
No enemy can stand in the day when the LORD Himself goes forth to war for His church.

etymology: Hebrew ’ophel, “a swelling” or “a fortified rise,” the strong hill in Jerusalem south of the temple mount; rendered “strong hold” of the daughter of Zion.
biblical_def: Ophel was a fortified rise, or strong hold, in Jerusalem, lying to the south of the temple mount and forming part of the defences of the city of God. There the Nethinims, the appointed servants of the temple, dwelt; for the record of Nehemiah’s wall says that the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, unto the place over against the water gate toward the east, and the tower that lieth out (Neh 3:26). The kings of Judah built it up for strength: Jotham built much on the wall of Ophel (2Chr 27:3), and after his repentance Manasseh compassed about Ophel and raised it up a very great height, putting captains of war in the fenced cities of Judah (2Chr 33:14). The prophet Micah gives the name its richest sense, calling it the strong hold of the daughter of Zion, unto whom the first dominion should come (Mic 4:8). So Ophel stands as a figure of the strength of the city of the great King, where the servants of the LORD dwelt under the shadow of His house. The dictionary records Ophel that the reader may see the church of God under the figure of a strong city, walled against her enemies. It witnesses that the true strong hold of the daughter of Zion is not her stones but her God, who is in the midst of her so that she shall not be moved, and who is Himself the tower of refuge to all who flee unto Him.
webster_summary: A fortified rise in Jerusalem south of the temple, where the Nethinims dwelt; the “strong hold” of Zion.
webster_full: OPHEL, a fortified hill or strong hold in Jerusalem, south of the temple mount.
The name signifies “a swelling” or “a fortified rise.”
There the Nethinims, the servants of the temple, dwelt in the days of Nehemiah.
Jotham and Manasseh built it up and raised it to a great height for defence.
Micah calls it the strong hold of the daughter of Zion.
scriptures: He built the high gate of the house of the LORD, and on the wall of Ophel he built much.

Now after this he built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entering in at the fish gate, and compassed about Ophel, and raised it up a very great height, and put captains of war in all the fenced cities of Judah.
Neh 3:26
Moreover the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, unto the place over against the water gate toward the east, and the tower that lieth out.
Mic 4:8
And thou, O tower of the flock, the strong hold of the daughter of Zion, unto thee shall it come, even the first dominion; the kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the strength of the city of God, whose true strong hold is the LORD Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Ophel is the fortified rise of Jerusalem, the strong shoulder of Zion where the temple servants dwelt and which the kings of Judah built up for defence. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it, and the dictionary records it that the reader may know it for a real stronghold of the holy city, named in the walls of Nehemiah and the songs of the prophets.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the true strong hold of the daughter of Zion is not her walls but her God. Micah called Ophel the strong hold of the daughter of Zion (Mic 4:8), yet the surer defence is the LORD who is in the midst of her, so that she shall not be moved (Psa 46:5). The church’s towers and bulwarks are worth telling to the generation following only because the God who set them is her everlasting refuge.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “a fortified rise,” Ophel names the strong hold of Zion south of the temple.
roots_lines: Ophel — Hebrew ’ophel, “a swelling” or “fortified rise.”
The word is from a root meaning “to swell” or “to be high.”
It named the strong hill in Jerusalem south of the temple mount.
There the Nethinims, servants of the temple, had their dwelling.
Micah renders it the “strong hold of the daughter of Zion.”
usage: Like Ophel, the church of God is a strong city, walled and towered against her enemies.
The true strong hold of Zion is not her stones but the LORD who dwells in her midst.
Mark well her bulwarks and tell her strength to the generation following, for her God is her refuge.

etymology: Hebrew millo’, “a filling” or “rampart,” from a root meaning “to fill,” the earthen filling or fortified mound built up in the city of David.
biblical_def: Millo, sometimes called the house of Millo, was a rampart or fortified filling in the city of David, a chief part of the defences of Jerusalem from the days of David onward. When David took the stronghold of Zion, he dwelt in the fort and called it the city of David, and built round about from Millo and inward (2Sam 5:9). Solomon raised a levy of labour to build the house of the LORD, his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem (1Ki 9:15), and the building of Millo and the repairing of the breaches of the city of David are named among his great works (1Ki 11:27). In the parallel record of David’s taking of the city, Joab repaired the rest of the city (1Chr 11:8). Long after, when Hezekiah prepared against the Assyrian, he repaired Millo in the city of David and strengthened all the broken wall (2Chr 32:5). Yet the name carries a darker memory also, for the servants who conspired against king Joash slew him in the house of Millo, which goeth down to Silla (2Ki 12:20). The dictionary records Millo that the reader may see the labour of generations spent upon the walls of the city of God, and the frailty of even a fortified throne where treachery may strike. It witnesses that the safety of Zion lies not in her ramparts but in the LORD, who is Himself a wall of fire round about His people.
webster_summary: A rampart or fortified filling in the city of David, built by David and Solomon and repaired by Hezekiah.
webster_full: MILLO, a rampart or earthen filling forming part of the defences of the city of David.
The name signifies “a filling” or “rampart,” from a root meaning “to fill.”
David built round about from Millo and inward when he took the stronghold of Zion.
Solomon raised a levy to build Millo and the wall of Jerusalem.
There king Joash was slain by his servants in the house of Millo.
scriptures: 2Sam 5:9
So David dwelt in the fort, and called it the city of David. And David built round about from Millo and inward.
And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the LORD, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer.
And this was the cause that he lifted up his hand against the king: Solomon built Millo, and repaired the breaches of the city of David his father.
And his servants arose, and made a conspiracy, and slew Joash in the house of Millo, which goeth down to Silla.
corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the safety of Zion lies not in her ramparts but in the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Millo is a rampart of the city of David, the fortified filling that David, Solomon, and Hezekiah laboured to build and to keep. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it, and the dictionary records it that the reader may know it for a real bulwark of the holy city, named through the long history of Jerusalem’s kings.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no rampart, however greatly raised, can be the true defence of the city of God. The same house of Millo that was built up for strength became the place where Joash was slain by treachery (2Ki 12:20); walls cannot save where the heart is false. The surer strength is the LORD who is in the midst of His church, so that she shall not be moved (Psa 46:5), and who is Himself the wall of fire round about His people.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “a filling” or “rampart,” Millo names the fortified mound of the city of David.
roots_lines: Millo — Hebrew millo’, “a filling” or “rampart.”
The word is from a root meaning “to fill” or “to make full.”
It named an earthen filling or fortified mound in the city of David.
David, Solomon, and Hezekiah built it up and repaired it for defence.
It is also called the house of Millo, where Joash was slain.
usage: Like Millo, the ramparts of the city of God are raised by the labour of many generations.
Yet no wall can save where the heart is false, as the slaying of Joash in Millo declares.
The true defence of Zion is the LORD, a wall of fire round about His people and the glory in their midst.
